subtopics: Stationary Distributions $\cdot$ Absorbing Chains $\cdot$ Pattern Waiting Times $\cdot$ Random Walks on Graphs
learningObjectives: **Define and classify Markov chains** — write the transition matrix, identify whether a chain is irreducible and aperiodic, and state the conditions for a unique stationary distribution.
**Find the stationary distribution** by solving $\pi P = \pi$ with $\sum_{i} \pi_{i} = 1$, and interpret it as the long-run fraction of time spent in each state.
**Use the stationary distribution to find expected return times**: $m_{i} = 1/\pi_{i}$ for any state $i$ in an irreducible aperiodic chain.
**Set up and solve absorbing chain problems** using the fundamental matrix $N = (I-Q)^{-1}$, including Gambler's Ruin and other stopping problems.
**Compute pattern waiting times** by designing a Markov chain whose states track progress toward the target pattern, then solving the resulting linear system.
**Compare pattern waiting times intuitively** — understand why HH takes longer than HT despite both having the same “naive” probability of occurring at each step.
**Analyse random walks on graphs** by setting up transition matrices and solving systems of equations for hitting probabilities.

sections.title: Introduction: Markov Chains in Quant Finance

blocks.content: A**Markov chain**isastochasticprocesswherethefuturedependsonthepresentstatealone,notonthehistory.Inquantfinance,Markovchainsmodelcreditratings,regimeswitches,orderbookstates,andmarketmicrostructure.Ininterviews,theyappearbothdirectly(“findthestationarydistribution”)anddisguised(“expectedtimetoseepatternHH”).

blocks.title: Markov Chain Fundamentals
blocks.content:
A (time-homogeneous, discrete-time) Markov chain on state space $\mathcal{S}$ is defined by the **transition matrix** $P$ with $P_{ij}= \mathbb{P}(X_{t+1}=j \mid X_{t}=i)$.

**Key properties:** \begin{itemize}\item **Irreducible:** every state is reachable from every other state. A finite irreducible chain has a *unique* stationary distribution.

\item **Aperiodic:** the GCD of return times to state $i$ is 1 for all $i$. Irreducible + aperiodic $\Rightarrow$ $P^{n} \to \mathbf{1}\pi^{\top}$ as $n\to\infty$.

\item **Stationary distribution** $\pi$: satisfies $\pi P = \pi$ and $\sum_{i} \pi_{i} = 1$.

\item **Expected return time:** for irreducible chains, $m_{i} = \mathbb{E}[\text{return time to }i] = 1/\pi_{i}$.\end{itemize}

blocks.title: Absorbing Chains and the Fundamental Matrix
Hitting Probabilities and Expected Hitting Times via Equations
blocks.content:
For most interview problems, writing a **linear system directly** is faster than inverting a matrix. Let $T$ be the first time the chain reaches a target set $A$.

**Hitting probability** $h_{i} = \mathbb{P}(T < \infty \mid X_{0} = i)$: \[h_{i} = \begin{cases}1&i \in A \\ \displaystyle\sum_{j} P_{ij}\,h_{j}&i \notin A\end{cases}\]

**Expected hitting time** $m_{i} = \mathbb{E}[T \mid X_{0} = i]$ (for states where $h_{i} = 1$): \[m_{i} = \begin{cases}0&i \in A \\ \displaystyle 1 + \sum_{j} P_{ij}\,m_{j}&i \notin A\end{cases}\]

**Practice:** For a random walk on $\{0,1,…,N\}$ absorbed at $0$ or $N$, these equations recover the Gambler's Ruin formula without matrix inversion. For pattern waiting times, the states track progress toward the pattern and the $m_{i}$ equations give the expected waiting time directly.

**Tip (from the *Green Book**):* Setting up and solving $m_{i}$ equations is the standard approach in most quant interview settings. The fundamental matrix $N=(I-Q)^{-1}$ is theoretically equivalent but requires matrix inversion, which is impractical by hand for chains with more than 3–4 transient states.

blocks.solution:
**(a) Transition matrix** (rows = current state, cols = next state): \[P = \bordermatrix{ & S & R \cr S & 0.8 & 0.2 \cr R & 0.4 & 0.6 }\]

**(b) Stationary distribution.** Solve $\pi P = \pi$, $\pi_{S} + \pi_{R} = 1$: \[\pi_{S} = 0.8\pi_{S} + 0.4\pi_{R} \implies 0.2\pi_{S} = 0.4\pi_{R} \implies \pi_{S} = 2\pi_{R}\] With $\pi_{S} + \pi_{R} = 1$: $2\pi_{R} + \pi_{R} = 1 \Rightarrow \pi_{R} = 1/3$, $\pi_{S} = 2/3$. \[\boxed{\pi = (2/3,\; 1/3)}\] **Interpretation:** In the long run, $2/3$ of days are Sunny and $1/3$ are Rainy.

**(c) Expected first passage time from S to R.** Let $h$ = expected days from Sunny until first Rainy day. Condition on the next day: \[h = 1 + 0.8\,h + 0.4\cdot0 \implies h - 0.8h = 1 \implies 0.2h = 1 \implies h = 5\] Starting Sunny, the expected wait for the first Rainy day is **5 days**.

**Note:** The expected return time to R from R is $1/\pi_{R} = 3$ days. Since R is visited on average every 3 days and sunny spells last on average 5 days (geometric with success prob $0.2$), these are consistent.

**Key takeaway:** For a 2-state chain with $P_{SR}=\alpha$ and $P_{RS}=\beta$: $\pi_{S} = \beta/(\alpha+\beta)$, $\pi_{R} = \alpha/(\alpha+\beta)$. Expected first passage from $S\to R$ is $1/\alpha$.

**(a) Stationary distribution.** Solve $\pi P = \pi$: \begin{align*}\pi_{1}&= \tfrac{1}{2}\pi_{2} \\ \pi_{2}&= \pi_{1} + \pi_{3} \\ \pi_{3}&= \tfrac{1}{2}\pi_{2}\end{align*} From the first and third equations: $\pi_{1} = \pi_{3} = \frac{1}{2}\pi_{2}$. With $\pi_{1}+\pi_{2}+\pi_{3}=1$: $\frac{1}{2}\pi_{2} + \pi_{2} + \frac{1}{2}\pi_{2}=1 \Rightarrow 2\pi_{2}=1 \Rightarrow \pi_{2} = 1/2$. \[\boxed{\pi = (1/4,\; 1/2,\; 1/4)}\]

**(b) Expected return times.** $m_{i} = 1/\pi_{i}$: \begin{itemize}\item $m_{1} = 4$ (state 1 is visited every 4 steps on average)

\item $m_{2} = 2$ (state 2 is visited every 2 steps)

\item $m_{3} = 4$\end{itemize}

**(c) Classification.** \begin{itemize}\item **Irreducible?** Yes: $1\to2\to3$ and $3\to2\to1$, so all states communicate.

\item **Aperiodic?** No. From state 1: the only way to return to 1 is $1\to2\to1$ (2 steps) or $1\to2\to3\to2\to1$ (4 steps), all even. So state 1 has period 2. The chain is **periodic with period 2**.\end{itemize}

**Consequence:** Despite being periodic, the unique stationary distribution still exists for this irreducible chain, and $m_{i} = 1/\pi_{i}$ still holds. However, $P^{n}$ does *not* converge to $\mathbf{1}\pi^{\top}$.

**Key takeaway:** Irreducibility guarantees a unique $\pi$ and the return-time formula. Aperiodicity is additionally needed for $P^{n}\to\mathbf{1}\pi^{\top}$.

**(a) Setup.** States: $\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}$. Absorbing: $\{0,5\}$. Transient: $\{1,2,3,4\}$.

Transition matrix (transient block $Q$, absorption block $R$): \[Q = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1/3 & 0 & 0 \\ 2/3 & 0 & 1/3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2/3 & 0 & 1/3 \\ 0 & 0 & 2/3 & 0\end{pmatrix},\quad R = \begin{pmatrix}2/3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/3\end{pmatrix}\]

**(b) Absorption probability via Gambler's Ruin formula.**

For $p\neq q$, the Gambler's Ruin formula gives the probability of reaching $N$ before 0, starting from $k$, with win prob $p$ per step: \[\mathbb{P}(\text{reach }N\text{ before }0 \mid X_{0}=k) = \frac{1-(q/p)^{k}}{1-(q/p)^{N}}\] Here $p=1/3$, $q=2/3$, $q/p=2$, $k=2$, $N=5$: \[\mathbb{P}(\text{ruin}^{c} \mid X_{0}=2) = \frac{1-2^{2}}{1-2^{5}}= \frac{1-4}{1-32}= \frac{-3}{-31}= \frac{3}{31}\approx 9.7\%\]

**(c) Expected duration.**

For the biased Gambler's Ruin, the expected duration from state $k$ is: \[\mathbb{E}[T \mid X_{0}=k] = \frac{k}{q-p}- \frac{N}{q-p}\cdot\frac{1-(q/p)^{k}}{1-(q/p)^{N}}\] With $p=1/3$, $q=2/3$, $q-p=1/3$, $N=5$, $k=2$, and $\mathbb{P}(\text{ruin}^{c} \mid X_{0}=2)=3/31$: \[\mathbb{E}[T\mid X_{0}=2] = 3k - 3N\cdot\frac{3}{31}= 6 - \frac{45}{31}= \frac{186-45}{31}= \frac{141}{31}\approx \boxed{4.55 \text{ steps}}\]

**Key takeaway:**

\begin{keyresult}{**Memorise** these two Gambler's Ruin formulas} Starting from $k$, absorbing barriers at $0$ and $N$, win prob $p$ per step ($q=1-p$, $p \neq q$): \[\underbrace{P_k = \frac{1-(q/p)^{k}}{1-(q/p)^{N}}}_{\text{probability of reaching }N}\qquad \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[T\mid X_0=k] = \frac{k}{q-p} - \frac{N}{q-p}\cdot P_k}_{\text{expected duration}}\] For $p=q=\tfrac{1}{2}$: $P_{k} = k/N$ and $\mathbb{E}[T\mid X_{0}=k] = k(N-k)$.\end{keyresult}

The matrix approach $(I-Q)^{-1}$ is more general but requires computation. Knowing both formulas by heart saves critical minutes in timed interviews.

blocks.content: ThemostcommonMarkovchaininterviewproblemsinvolvewaitingforaspecificpatterninasequenceofcoinflips.Thekeytechniqueisdesigningachainwhosestatestrack*progress toward the pattern*.

blocks.title: Pattern Waiting Time via Markov Chain
blocks.content:
To find the expected number of flips until pattern $W$ first appears: \begin{enumerate}\item Define states as the length of the longest suffix of the sequence so far that is also a prefix of $W$.

\item Write the transition equations $e_{i} = 1 + \sum_{j} P_{ij}e_{j}$ where state “done” has $e = 0$.

\item Solve the linear system.\end{enumerate} Alternatively, use the **optional stopping theorem** with a martingale.

blocks.solution:
**(a) Expected time for HH.**

States: $\{0,\text{H},\text{HH}\}$ where 0=start/just saw T, H=just saw H (1 H so far), HH=done.

Let $e_{0}$ = expected flips from state 0, $e_{H}$ from state H. \[e_{0} = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{H} + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{0} \qquad\text{(H: go to H; T: stay at 0)}\] \[e_{H} = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot0 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{0} \qquad\text{(H: done; T: go to 0)}\] From the first equation: $\frac{1}{2}e_{0} = 1 + \frac{1}{2}e_{H} \Rightarrow e_{0} = 2 + e_{H}$. Substituting into the second: $e_{H} = 1 + \frac{1}{2}(2+e_{H}) = 2 + \frac{1}{2}e_{H} \Rightarrow e_{H} = 4$. So $e_{0} = 6$.

\[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T_{HH}] = 6}\]

**(b) Expected time for HT.**

States: $\{0,\text{H},\text{HT}\}$. From 0: H (prob 1/2)$\to$H, T (prob 1/2)$\to$0. From H: T (1/2)$\to$done, H (1/2)$\to$H (stay!). \[e_{0} = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{H} + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{0} \implies e_{0} = 2 + e_{H}\] \[e_{H} = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot0 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{H} \implies \tfrac{1}{2}e_{H} = 1 \implies e_{H} = 2\] So $e_{0} = 4$. \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T_{HT}] = 4}\]

**(c) Intuitive explanation.**

$\mathbb{E}[T_{HT}] = 4 < \mathbb{E}[T_{HH}] = 6$.

When waiting for HH: if you've just seen H and the next flip is T, you've “wasted” the H and must start completely over from state 0.

When waiting for HT: if you've just seen H and the next flip is H, you haven't wasted anything — you're still in state H, still one flip away from completing HT. The pattern HT is *self-reinforcing* (a new H while in state H keeps you at state H), while HH is *self-defeating* (a T after H sends you back to the start).

**Key takeaway:** Pattern waiting times depend critically on *overlaps*. HT has no overlap (T cannot start a new HT pattern), while HH overlaps with itself (HH contains H as a prefix). Patterns with larger self-overlap take longer on average.

blocks.content: **Winning Probability in an Alternating Pattern Game.** Players A and B alternate flipping a fair coin (A starts). If the pattern HT appears (head immediately followed by tail), the player who flips the tail wins. What is $\mathbb{P}(A\text{ wins})$?
blocks.solution:
**States.** Track the last flip and whose turn it is next. Define five states: \begin{itemize}\item **S**: Start (no flip yet), A's turn.

\item **AH**: A just flipped H; B's turn next.

\item **BH**: B just flipped H; A's turn next.

\item **BT**: last flip was T (by B); B's turn next.

\item **AT**: last flip was T (by A); A's turn next.\end{itemize}

**Transitions.** The game ends when a T is flipped immediately after an H (forming HT); the tail-flipper wins. \begin{itemize}\item From **AH** (B flips): T(1/2)$\to$**B wins**; H(1/2)$\to$BH.

\item From **BH** (A flips): T(1/2)$\to$**A wins**; H(1/2)$\to$AH.

\item From **BT** (B flips): H(1/2)$\to$BH; T(1/2)$\to$AT.

\item From **AT** (A flips): H(1/2)$\to$AH; T(1/2)$\to$BT.

\item From **S** (A flips): H(1/2)$\to$AH; T(1/2)$\to$BT.\end{itemize}

**Equations.** Let $p_{X}$ = Prob(A wins from state $X$). \[p_{\text{AH}}= \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot0 + \tfrac{1}{2}\,p_{\text{BH}}= \tfrac{p_{\text{BH}}}{2}\] \[p_{\text{BH}}= \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\,p_{\text{AH}}= \tfrac{1}{2}+ \tfrac{p_{\text{AH}}}{2}\] Solving: $p_{\text{AH}}=\tfrac{1}{3}$,\; $p_{\text{BH}}=\tfrac{2}{3}$.

\[p_{\text{BT}}= \tfrac{1}{2}p_{\text{BH}}+ \tfrac{1}{2}p_{\text{AT}}= \tfrac{1}{3}+ \tfrac{p_{\text{AT}}}{2}\] \[p_{\text{AT}}= \tfrac{1}{2}p_{\text{AH}}+ \tfrac{1}{2}p_{\text{BT}}= \tfrac{1}{6}+ \tfrac{p_{\text{BT}}}{2}\] Substituting: $p_{\text{BT}}= \tfrac{1}{3}+\tfrac{1}{12}+\tfrac{p_{\text{BT}}}{4}\Rightarrow \tfrac{3}{4}p_{\text{BT}}=\tfrac{5}{12}\Rightarrow p_{\text{BT}}=\tfrac{5}{9}$.

From Start (A first flips): \[p_{S} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,p_{\text{AH}}+ \tfrac{1}{2}\,p_{\text{BT}}= \tfrac{1}{6}+ \tfrac{5}{18}= \boxed{\dfrac{4}{9}}\]

**Key takeaway:** Despite A going first, A wins with probability $4/9 < 1/2$. After a T is flipped (by either player), the situation is not symmetric — it matters whose turn it is next, since only the player who flips T after an H wins. The full 5-state chain is needed to capture this.

**(a) $\mathbb{E}[T_{HH**] = 6$} from Problem 4(a).

**(b) $\mathbb{E}[T_{HHH**]$.}

States: 0 = (no progress), H = (1 H so far), HH = (2 H so far), done.

Let $e_{0}, e_{1}, e_{2}$ be expected remaining flips from each state: \begin{align*}e_{0}&= 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{1} + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{0} \implies e_{0} = 2 + e_{1} \\ e_{1}&= 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{0} \\ e_{2}&= 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot0 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{0} \implies e_{2} = 1 + \tfrac{e_0}{2}\end{align*} Substitute $e_{2}$ into $e_{1}$: $e_{1} = 1 + \frac{1}{2}(1+\frac{e_{0}}{2}) + \frac{e_{0}}{2}= \frac{3}{2}+ \frac{3e_{0}}{4}$. Then $e_{0} = 2 + \frac{3}{2}+ \frac{3e_{0}}{4}\Rightarrow \frac{e_{0}}{4}= \frac{7}{2}\Rightarrow e_{0} = 14$. \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T_{HHH}] = 14}\]

**(c) General formula.**

Let $e_{k}$ = expected flips from state $k$ (already have $k$ consecutive heads). The recurrence is: $e_{k} = 1 + \frac{1}{2}e_{k+1}+ \frac{1}{2}e_{0}$ for $k < n$, with $e_{n} = 0$.

By induction (or by noticing the pattern), solving this system gives: \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T_{H^n}] = 2^{n+1} - 2 = 2(2^n - 1)}\]

**Verify:** $n=1$: $\mathbb{E}[T_{H}] = 2$. ✓\; $n=2$: $6$. ✓\; $n=3$: $14$. ✓

**Intuitive derivation:** Use the tower argument. $\mathbb{E}[T_{H^n}] = \mathbb{E}[T_{H^{n-1}}] + \mathbb{E}[\text{additional flips for last H}]$. Given we've just achieved $H^{n-1}$, the next flip is H (prob 1/2, done) or T (prob 1/2, restart from scratch). So: $\mathbb{E}[T_{H^n}] = \mathbb{E}[T_{H^{n-1}}] + 1 + \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[T_{H^n}]$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[T_{H^n}] = \mathbb{E}[T_{H^{n-1}}] + 1$ $\Rightarrow \mathbb{E}[T_{H^n}] = 2\mathbb{E}[T_{H^{n-1}}] + 2$.

Solving this recurrence with $\mathbb{E}[T_{H^0}]=0$: $\mathbb{E}[T_{H^n}] = 2^{n+1}-2$.

blocks.content: **Expected Waiting Time for Consecutive Dice Outcomes.** Roll a fair six-sided die repeatedly. Find the expected number of rolls until you see two consecutive 5's. Generalise to $n$ consecutive 5's.
blocks.solution:
**Expected rolls until two consecutive 5's.**

States: 0 (no 5 just rolled), 1 (last roll was 5), done. Let $e_{0}, e_{1}$ be expected rolls from each state. \[e_{0} = 1 + \tfrac{1}{6}e_{1} + \tfrac{5}{6}e_{0} \implies \tfrac{1}{6}e_{0} = 1 + \tfrac{1}{6}e_{1} \implies e_{0} = 6 + e_{1}\] \[e_{1} = 1 + \tfrac{1}{6}\cdot0 + \tfrac{5}{6}e_{0}\] Substitute $e_{0} = 6+e_{1}$: $e_{1} = 1 + \frac{5}{6}(6+e_{1}) = 1 + 5 + \frac{5}{6}e_{1} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{6}e_{1} = 6 \Rightarrow e_{1} = 36$. So $e_{0} = 42$. \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T_{\text{two 5's}}] = 42}\]

**General formula for $n$ consecutive 5's.**

The recurrence mirrors the coin case. Let $p = 1/6$ (prob of 5), $q = 5/6$. Using the same tower argument: \[\mathbb{E}[T_{n}] = 2\mathbb{E}[T_{n-1}] + \frac{1}{p}\quad\text{with}\quad \mathbb{E}[T_{0}] = 0\] Wait: let us redo. Given $n-1$ consecutive 5's, the next roll: \begin{itemize}\item 5 (prob $p$): done. Additional: $1$ roll.

\item Not 5 (prob $1-p$): restart from 0. Additional: $1 + \mathbb{E}[T_{n}]$.\end{itemize} So $\mathbb{E}[T_{n}] = \mathbb{E}[T_{n-1}] + 1 + (1-p)\mathbb{E}[T_{n}] \Rightarrow p\,\mathbb{E}[T_{n}] = \mathbb{E}[T_{n-1}] + 1 \Rightarrow \mathbb{E}[T_{n}] = \frac{\mathbb{E}[T_{n-1}]+1}{p}$.

Solving: $\mathbb{E}[T_{n}] = \frac{1}{p}+ \frac{1}{p^{2}}+ \cdots + \frac{1}{p^{n}}= \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{p^{k}}$.

\[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T_n] = \frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{p^{2}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{p^{n}} = \frac{(1/p)^{n+1}-1/p}{1/p-1} = \frac{1-p^{n}}{p^{n}(1-p)}}\]

**Verify for die ($p=1/6$, $n=2$):** $\mathbb{E}[T_{2}] = 6 + 36 = 42$. ✓\quad For coin ($p=1/2$, $n=2$): $\mathbb{E}[T_{2}]=2+4=6$. ✓

**Key takeaway:** The general formula $\mathbb{E}[T_{n}]=\sum_{k=1}^{n} p^{-k}$ applies to any i.i.d.\ sequence with success probability $p$.

blocks.content: **First Occurrence of HH vs TH in Coin Tossing.** Flip a fair coin until either HH or TH appears as two consecutive flips. If HH appears first you win. Find $\mathbb{P}(\text{you win})$. Can the answer be determined by a symmetry argument?
blocks.solution:
**States.** Track the last flip. \begin{itemize}\item **S**: Start (no flip yet).

\item **H**: last flip was H.

\item **T**: last flip was T.\end{itemize}

**Transitions.** \begin{itemize}\item From **S**: H(1/2)$\to$H;\; T(1/2)$\to$T.

\item From **H**: H(1/2)$\to$**HH: you win**;\; T(1/2)$\to$**TH: you lose**.

\item From **T**: H(1/2)$\to$**TH: you lose**;\; T(1/2)$\to$T (stay).\end{itemize}

**Key observation.** State T is a *death trap*: once the last flip is T, the next H completes TH (you lose), and the next T keeps you in state T. You can never win from state T.

**Equations.** Let $p_{X}$ = Prob(you win from state $X$). \[p_{T} = \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot0 + \tfrac{1}{2}\,p_{T} \implies p_{T} = 0\] \[p_{H} = \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot0 = \tfrac{1}{2}\] \[p_{S} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,p_{H} + \tfrac{1}{2}\,p_{T} = \tfrac{1}{4}+ 0 = \boxed{\dfrac{1}{4}}\]

**Why the symmetry argument fails.** Both HH and TH end with H, so one might argue the game ends equally on HH or TH. But this ignores that once a T is ever flipped, every future path through state T leads to a loss — the state T is absorbing into a loss. The only winning path is H on flip 1, H on flip 2 (probability $\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{4}$).

**Key takeaway:** Despite the symmetric-looking patterns, HH and TH are not equally likely to appear first. Once a T occurs, TH wins with certainty. You win only via the path $S\to H\to\text{HH}$, giving probability $\mathbf{1/4}$.

blocks.content:
**Which Pattern Appears First in Coin Tossing?** Flip a fair coin repeatedly. Find: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic{*})]\item $\mathbb{P}(\text{HHT appears before HTT})$

\item $\mathbb{P}(\text{HHT appears before HTH})$

\item $\mathbb{P}(\text{HHH appears before THH})$

\item $\mathbb{P}(\text{HHT appears before THH})$\end{enumerate}
blocks.solution:
**Method.** Build a Markov chain whose states are the set of possible “current progress” prefixes toward either pattern. Write transition equations and solve.

**(1) HHT vs HTT.**

States track the longest common suffix that is a prefix of HHT or HTT. The shared prefix H means: after first H, we're at state H for both. From H: next flip H$\to$HH (toward HHT), T$\to$HT (toward HTT). From HH: T$\to$HHT (done, HHT wins); H$\to$HH (stay). From HT: T$\to$HTT (done, HTT wins); H$\to$H (restart).

Let $p_{i}$ = Prob(HHT wins from state $i$). \begin{align*}p_{\text{start}}&= \tfrac{1}{2}p_{H} + \tfrac{1}{2}p_{\text{start}}\implies p_{\text{start}}= p_{H} \\ p_{H}&= \tfrac{1}{2}p_{HH}+ \tfrac{1}{2}p_{HT}\\ p_{HH}&= \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot1 + \tfrac{1}{2}p_{HH}\implies p_{HH}= 1 \\ p_{HT}&= \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot0 + \tfrac{1}{2}p_{H}\end{align*} From $p_{H} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot1 + \frac{1}{2}p_{HT}$ and $p_{HT}= \frac{1}{2}p_{H}$: $p_{H} = \frac{1}{2}+ \frac{1}{4}p_{H} \Rightarrow \frac{3}{4}p_{H} = \frac{1}{2}\Rightarrow p_{H} = 2/3$.

$\boxed{\mathbb{P}(\text{HHT before HTT}) = 2/3}$

**(2) HHT vs HTH.** Similar analysis (left as exercise): $\mathbb{P}(\text{HHT before HTH}) = \boxed{2/3}$.

**(3) HHH vs THH.**

After the first H: both patterns need HH next. The key difference: \begin{itemize}\item From state H: next H$\to$HH, next T$\to$start (for HHH), but T$\to$ “T-seen” for THH.

\item THH is achieved via T then HH.\end{itemize}

States: \{start, T, H, TH, HH, THH=done(THH wins), HHH=done(HHH wins)\}. Let $p$ = Prob(HHH wins) from start:

From start: H(1/2)$\to$H; T(1/2)$\to$T. From H: H(1/2)$\to$HH; T(1/2)$\to$T. From HH: H(1/2)$\to$HHH(win); T(1/2)$\to$T. From T: H(1/2)$\to$TH; T(1/2)$\to$T. From TH: H(1/2)$\to$THH(lose); T(1/2)$\to$T.

Let $p_{s},p_{T},p_{H},p_{HH},p_{TH}$ be winning probs from each state. $p_{HH}= 1/2$, $p_{TH}=0$. $p_{T} = \frac{1}{2}p_{TH}+\frac{1}{2}p_{T} \Rightarrow p_{T}=0$. $p_{H} = \frac{1}{2}p_{HH}+\frac{1}{2}p_{T} = \frac{1}{4}$. $p_{s} = \frac{1}{2}p_{H} + \frac{1}{2}p_{T} = \frac{1}{8}$.

$\boxed{\mathbb{P}(\text{HHH before THH}) = 1/8}$

**(4) HHT vs THH.**

**States:** S (start), H, HH, T, TH. Winning patterns: HHT (we win); THH (we lose).

Key observations: \begin{itemize}\item From **T** or **TH**: the next H gives TH or THH (we lose); the next T stays in T. So $p_{T} = p_{TH}= 0$ — state T is a death trap for us.

\item From **HH**: next T $\to$ HHT (win); next H $\to$ HH. So $p_{HH}=1$.

\item From **H**: H$\to$HH ($p=1$); T$\to$T ($p=0$). $p_{H} = \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot0 = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

\item From **S**: H$\to$H; T$\to$T. $p_{S} = \tfrac{1}{2}p_{H} + \tfrac{1}{2}p_{T} = \tfrac{1}{4}$.\end{itemize}

$\boxed{\mathbb{P}(\text{HHT before THH}) = 1/4}$

Once a T appears before HH is reached, THH wins with certainty. The only winning path is $S\to H\to HH\to\text{HHT}$, with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}\times\tfrac{1}{2}\times1 = \tfrac{1}{4}$.

**Key takeaway:** Pattern-vs-pattern races are highly non-intuitive. The Conway leading number method provides a systematic approach: compute the overlap score for each pattern pair to determine which pattern tends to appear first.

blocks.content: **Waiting Time for the Pattern HTH.** Flip a fair coin repeatedly. Find $\mathbb{E}[T_{HTH}]$ — the expected number of flips until the pattern HTH first appears.
blocks.solution:
**States.** Track the longest suffix of flips so far that is also a prefix of HTH: \begin{itemize}\item State 0: no progress (or last flip was T after state 0). \item State H: last flip was H (matches prefix “H” of HTH). \item State HT: last two flips were HT (matches prefix “HT”). \item State HTH: done.\end{itemize} **Transitions from each state:**
StateFlip H (prob 1/2)Flip T (prob 1/2)
0$\to$ H$\to$ 0
H$\to$ H$\to$ HT
HT$\to$ HTH (done!)$\to$ 0
**Note:** From state H, flipping H keeps you at H (not 0!) because the new H could be the start of a new HTH. From state HT, flipping T goes to 0 (not HT—T is not a prefix of HTH). **Expected flip equations.** Let $e_{0}, e_{H}, e_{HT}$ be expected flips to completion from each state: \begin{align*}e_{0}&= 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{H} + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{0} \implies e_{0} = 2 + e_{H} \\ e_{H}&= 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{H} + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{HT}\implies \tfrac{1}{2}e_{H} = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{HT}\implies e_{H} = 2 + e_{HT}\\ e_{HT}&= 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot0 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{0} \implies e_{HT}= 1 + \tfrac{e_0}{2}\end{align*} **Solve:** $e_{H} = 2 + e_{HT}= 2 + 1 + \frac{e_{0}}{2}= 3 + \frac{e_{0}}{2}$. $e_{0} = 2 + e_{H} = 2 + 3 + \frac{e_{0}}{2}= 5 + \frac{e_{0}}{2}$. $\frac{e_{0}}{2}= 5 \Rightarrow e_{0} = 10$. \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T_{HTH}] = 10}\] **Key takeaway:** The state transitions for HTH are non-trivial because “H” overlaps with itself as a prefix of HTH. Always redraw the state diagram carefully, especially the self-loops and “partial-match” transitions.

blocks.content: **Waiting Time for the Pattern HHHHT.** Flip a fair coin repeatedly. Find $\mathbb{E}[T_{HHHHT}]$ — the expected number of flips until the pattern HHHHT first appears.
blocks.solution:
**States:** 0, H, HH, HHH, HHHH, done (HHHHT). **Transitions:**
StateH (prob 1/2)T (prob 1/2)
0$\to$ H$\to$ 0
H$\to$ HH$\to$ 0
HH$\to$ HHH$\to$ 0
HHH$\to$ HHHH$\to$ 0
HHHH$\to$ HHHH$\to$ done
Note: from state HHHH, flipping H keeps you at HHHH (still four H's). Flipping T completes HHHHT. **Equations.** Let $e_{0}, e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}, e_{4}$ for states 0, H, HH, HHH, HHHH: \begin{align*}e_{0}&= 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{1} + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{0} \implies e_{0} = 2 + e_{1} \\ e_{1}&= 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{0} \\ e_{2}&= 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{3} + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{0} \\ e_{3}&= 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{4} + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{0} \\ e_{4}&= 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{4} + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot0 \implies \tfrac{1}{2}e_{4} = 1 \implies e_{4} = 2\end{align*} **Back-substitute** (using $e_{4} = 2$ throughout): \begin{align*}e_{3}&= 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}(2) + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{0} = 2 + \tfrac{e_0}{2}\\ e_{2}&= 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(2+\tfrac{e_0}{2}\right) + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{0} = 2 + \tfrac{3e_0}{4}\\ e_{1}&= 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(2+\tfrac{3e_0}{4}\right) + \tfrac{1}{2}e_{0} = 2 + \tfrac{7e_0}{8}\end{align*} From $e_{0} = 2 + e_{1}$: \[e_{0} = 2 + 2 + \frac{7e_{0}}{8}= 4 + \frac{7e_{0}}{8}\implies \frac{e_{0}}{8}= 4 \implies e_{0} = 32\] **Verify:** $e_{1} = 30$, $e_{2} = 26$, $e_{3} = 18$, $e_{4} = 2$. Check $e_{0} = 2+e_{1} = 32$ ✓;\; $e_{3} = 2 + 16 = 18$ ✓. \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[T_{HHHHT}] = 32}\] **Connection to the general formula.** From Topic 8 Problem~6, $\mathbb{E}[T_{H^n}] = 2^{n+1}-2$, so $\mathbb{E}[T_{HHHH}] = 30$. The extra tail adds $e_{4} = 2$ steps on top: $30 + 2 = 32$. ✓ **Key takeaway:** State HHHH self-loops on H, making $e_{4} = 2$ (a geometric$(1/2)$ wait for the first T). Back-substitution from $e_{4}$ through $e_{0}$ gives $32$ cleanly without any matrix inversion.

**State machine.** Track progress toward both patterns simultaneously. Let the state encode the longest suffix seen that is a prefix of HHT and/or HTH:
StateDescriptionHHT prefixHTH prefix
$s_{0}$No useful progress$\varepsilon$$\varepsilon$
$s_{1}$Last flip was HHH
$s_{2}$Last two were HHHHH
$s_{3}$Last two were HT$\varepsilon$HT
**Transitions:**
FromFlip H ($\tfrac{1{2}$)}Flip T ($\tfrac{1{2}$)}
$s_{0}$$s_{1}$$s_{0}$
$s_{1}$$s_{2}$$s_{3}$
$s_{2}$$s_{2}$HHT wins
$s_{3}$HTH wins$s_{0}$
**(a) Probability HHT wins.** Let $p_{i} = \mathbb{P}(\text{HHT wins}\mid s_{i})$. \begin{align*}p_{0}&= \tfrac{1}{2}p_{1} + \tfrac{1}{2}p_{0}&\implies p_{0}&= p_{1} \\ p_{1}&= \tfrac{1}{2}p_{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}p_{3} \\ p_{2}&= \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot1 + \tfrac{1}{2}p_{2}&\implies p_{2}&= 1 \\ p_{3}&= \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot0 + \tfrac{1}{2}p_{0}&\implies p_{3}&= \tfrac{p_0}{2}\end{align*} Substituting into $p_{1} = p_{0}$: $p_{0} = \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{p_0}{2}= \tfrac{1}{2}+ \tfrac{p_0}{4}\implies \tfrac{3}{4}p_{0} = \tfrac{1}{2}\implies \boxed{p_0 = \tfrac{2}{3}}$. **(b) Conditional expected time given HHT wins.** Let $f_{i} = \mathbb{E}[T\cdot\mathbf{1}_{\text{HHT wins}}\mid s_{i}]$ (the “weighted” expected time; divide by $p_{i}$ at the end). Each step costs 1 flip, so the recurrence is: $f_{i} = \sum_{j} P_{ij}(p_{j} + f_{j})$ for non-absorbing states, with the absorbing step contributing its terminal probability. \begin{align*}f_{2}&= \tfrac{1}{2}(1\cdot1 + 0) + \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + f_{2}) = 1 + \tfrac{f_2}{2}&\implies f_{2}&= 2 \\ f_{3}&= \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(p_{0} + f_{0})&\implies f_{3}&= \tfrac{1}{3}+ \tfrac{f_0}{2}\\ f_{1}&= \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + f_{2}) + \tfrac{1}{2}(p_{3} + f_{3}) &= \tfrac{3}{2}+ \tfrac{1}{6}+ \tfrac{f_3}{2}= \tfrac{5}{3}+ \tfrac{f_3}{2}\\ f_{0}&= \tfrac{1}{2}(p_{1} + f_{1}) + \tfrac{1}{2}(p_{0} + f_{0}) \implies f_{0} = p_{0} + p_{1} + f_{1} = \tfrac{4}{3}+ f_{1}\end{align*} Solving: $f_{3} = \tfrac{1}{3}+ \tfrac{f_0}{2}$,\; $f_{1} = \tfrac{5}{3}+ \tfrac{1}{2}(\tfrac{1}{3}+ \tfrac{f_0}{2}) = \tfrac{11}{6}+ \tfrac{f_0}{4}$,\; $f_{0} = \tfrac{4}{3}+ \tfrac{11}{6}+ \tfrac{f_0}{4}\implies \tfrac{3f_0}{4}= \tfrac{19}{6}\implies f_{0} = \tfrac{38}{9}$. \[\mathbb{E}[T \mid \text{HHT wins}] = \frac{f_{0}}{p_{0}}= \frac{38/9}{2/3}= \boxed{\dfrac{19}{3} \approx 6.33}\] **(c) Conditional expected time given HTH wins.** By symmetry of the $f_{i}$ construction with HTH-winning weights, $g_{0} = \mathbb{E}[T\cdot\mathbf{1}_{\text{HTH wins}}\mid s_{0}] = \tfrac{16}{9}$ (analogous calculation), and $\mathbb{P}(\text{HTH wins}) = \tfrac{1}{3}$. \[\mathbb{E}[T \mid \text{HTH wins}] = \frac{g_{0}}{1-p_{0}}= \frac{16/9}{1/3}= \boxed{\dfrac{16}{3} \approx 5.33}\] **Sanity check:** $\mathbb{E}[T] = f_{0} + g_{0} = \tfrac{38}{9}+\tfrac{16}{9}= \tfrac{54}{9}= 6$. This matches the unconditional expected time to one of $\{\text{HHT, HTH}\}$, computed directly from the same state machine. ✓ **Key takeaway:** Conditional expected times use $f_{i} = \mathbb{E}[T\cdot\mathbf{1}_{A}]$, then divide by $p_{i} = \mathbb{P}(A)$. The weighted recurrence $f_{i} = \sum_{j} P_{ij}(p_{j} + f_{j})$ captures both the cost of the current step and the probability-weighted future costs. Strikingly, HTH wins *faster on average* ($16/3$) than HHT ($19/3$), even though HHT is more likely to win. Once HHT is on course (past state $s_{2}$), it may spin there for extra H's before seeing the needed T.

blocks.content: **Meeting Probability for Two Random-Walking Ants on an Octahedron.** Two ants start at opposite vertices of a regular octahedron. Each turn: Ant A moves first to a uniformly random adjacent vertex, then Ant B moves to a uniformly random adjacent vertex. They stop when one ant moves onto the vertex occupied by the other. What is $\mathbb{P}(\text{A moves onto B's vertex})$?
blocks.solution:
**Octahedron structure.** A regular octahedron has 6 vertices, each of degree 4. Label two opposite poles $N$ (A starts) and $S$ (B starts). The remaining 4 vertices are *equatorial* and lie on a 4-cycle $v$–$w$–$u$–$x$–$v$. Every equatorial vertex is adjacent to both poles and to its two equatorial cycle-neighbours; it is *not* adjacent to the equatorial vertex opposite it on the 4-cycle.

**States** (relative position of A and B after each full turn): \begin{itemize}\item **Opp**: A and B are at opposite vertices.

\item **Adj**: A and B are at adjacent vertices.\end{itemize} The game starts in state **Opp**.

**Let** $p = \mathbb{P}(\text{A catches B first}\mid\text{Opp})$, $q = \mathbb{P}(\text{A catches B first}\mid\text{Adj})$.

\medskip **From Opp** (A at $N$, B at $S$).

A moves first: all 4 of $N$'s neighbours are equatorial, none is $S$, so A *cannot* catch B. A lands on some equatorial vertex $v$.

B then moves from $S$: $S$'s 4 neighbours are all equatorial. \begin{itemize}\item B moves to $v$ (prob $\tfrac{1}{4}$): B lands on A — B wins.

\item B moves to an equatorial neighbour of $v$ on the 4-cycle (prob $\tfrac{2}{4}$): A and B are now adjacent $\to$ state **Adj**.

\item B moves to the equatorial vertex opposite $v$ (prob $\tfrac{1}{4}$): A and B are now opposite $\to$ state **Opp**.\end{itemize} \[p = 0\cdot\tfrac{1}{4}+ q\cdot\tfrac{2}{4}+ p\cdot\tfrac{1}{4}\;\implies\; \tfrac{3p}{4}= \tfrac{q}{2}\;\implies\; \boxed{p = \tfrac{2q}{3}}\tag{1}\]

\medskip **From Adj** (A at equatorial $v$, B at equatorial $w$, with $v$–$w$ an edge).

Label the 4-cycle $v$–$w$–$u$–$x$–$v$, so $v$'s octahedron neighbours are $\{N,S,w,x\}$ and $w$'s are $\{N,S,v,u\}$.

A moves first (4 equally likely destinations):

\begin{itemize}\item **A$\to w$** (prob $\tfrac{1}{4}$): A lands on B — **A wins**.

\item **A$\to N$** (prob $\tfrac{1}{4}$): A at $N$, B at $w$ (adjacent, since $N$ adj to all equatorial). B moves from $w$ to $\{N,S,v,u\}$: \begin{itemize}\item $B\to N$ ($\tfrac{1}{4}$): B catches A — B wins (contrib 0).

\item $B\to S$ ($\tfrac{1}{4}$): A at $N$, B at $S$ $\to$ **Opp**.

\item $B\to v$ ($\tfrac{1}{4}$): A at $N$, B at $v$ $\to$ **Adj**.

\item $B\to u$ ($\tfrac{1}{4}$): A at $N$, B at $u$ $\to$ **Adj**.\end{itemize} Contribution: $\tfrac{1}{4}(0 + p + q + q) = \tfrac{p+2q}{4}$.

\item **A$\to S$** (prob $\tfrac{1}{4}$): symmetric to A$\to N$. Contribution: $\tfrac{p+2q}{4}$.

\item **A$\to x$** (prob $\tfrac{1}{4}$): A at $x$, B at $w$. $x$ and $w$ are opposite on the 4-cycle (2 steps apart), hence opposite vertices of the octahedron. B moves from $w$ to $\{N,S,v,u\}$; none of these equals $x$ (B cannot catch A). $x$ is adjacent to $N$, $S$, $v$, $u$ — all of B's possible destinations — so the resulting state is **Adj** in all 4 cases. Contribution: $\tfrac{1}{4}(q+q+q+q) = q$.\end{itemize}

Assembling (each A-move has weight $\tfrac{1}{4}$): \[q = \tfrac{1}{4}\!\cdot\!1 + \tfrac{1}{4}\!\cdot\!\tfrac{p+2q}{4}+ \tfrac{1}{4}\!\cdot\!\tfrac{p+2q}{4}+ \tfrac{1}{4}\!\cdot\! q = \tfrac{1}{4}+ \tfrac{p+2q}{8}+ \tfrac{q}{4}\] \[q - \tfrac{q}{4}= \tfrac{1}{4}+ \tfrac{p}{8}+ \tfrac{q}{4}\;\implies\; \tfrac{q}{2}= \tfrac{1}{4}+ \tfrac{p}{8}\;\implies\; \boxed{q = \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{p}{4}}\tag{2}\]

**Solving (1) and (2).** Substitute $p = \tfrac{2q}{3}$ into (2): \[q = \tfrac{1}{2}+ \tfrac{1}{4}\cdot\tfrac{2q}{3}= \tfrac{1}{2}+ \tfrac{q}{6}\;\implies\; \tfrac{5q}{6}= \tfrac{1}{2}\;\implies\; q = \tfrac{3}{5}, \quad p = \tfrac{2}{3}\cdot\tfrac{3}{5}= \tfrac{2}{5}\]

\[\boxed{\mathbb{P}(\text{A catches B first}) = \dfrac{2}{5}}\]

**Sanity checks.** $p = 2/5 < 1/2$: A is at a slight disadvantage because B *reacts* after A's move, so B sometimes catches A before A can reverse and catch B. $q = 3/5 > 1/2$: from Adjacent, A can immediately land on B (prob 1/4), giving A an advantage.

**Key takeaway:** Set up relative-position states (Opp / Adj) and track who catches whom in each half-turn. The key equation from Opp gives $p = 2q/3$; the careful A$\to x$ branch (landing in Opp, but B's moves all yield Adj) is what distinguishes this from a simpler chain.

**Topic 8 Technique Toolkit**
Stationary distributionSolve $\pi P=\pi$, $\sum\pi_{i}=1$. For 2-state: $\pi_{i} = p_{ji}/(p_{ij}+p_{ji})$.
Expected return time$m_{i} = 1/\pi_{i}$ for irreducible chains.
PeriodicityPeriod = GCD of return times. Irreducible + period 1 = ergodic.
Absorbing chains$N=(I-Q)^{-1}$; absorption probs $B=NR$; expected time $t=N\mathbf{1}$.
Gambler's Ruin (biased)$P_{k} = (1-(q/p)^{k})/(1-(q/p)^{N})$. Expected duration: $k/(q-p) - N P_{k}/(q-p)$.
Pattern waiting: statesStates = length of longest suffix that is a prefix of target. Write $e_{i} = 1 + \sum P_{ij}e_{j}$ and solve.
HH vs HT$\mathbb{E}[T_{HH}]=6$, $\mathbb{E}[T_{HT}]=4$. Self-overlap makes HH slower.
$n$ consecutive (prob $p$)$\mathbb{E}[T_{n}]=\sum_{k=1}^{n} p^{-k}$. For fair coin: $2^{n+1}-2$.
Pattern raceBuild a combined chain; solve for absorption probability. Conway's method: compare overlap scores.
Graph random walksReduce by symmetry to equivalence classes. Set up hitting-probability equations.
